item.title: As Political Ad Spending Skyrockets, Broadcast TV Remains King
item.description:
The deluge of political advertising in this year’s midterm elections is shattering previous records.

Almost half of that money is going to a surprising place: your local TV channel.

Advertisers, following the changing viewing habits of Americans, have increasingly shifted their marketing dollars to social platforms, streaming channels and other digital media. Yet when it comes to federal and state races, politicians and PACs are brushing aside concerns that TV ads are costlier to produce and less efficient in targeting prospective voters — and are showering local stations with billions of dollars.

This election will show how much that calculus still holds in a transformed media environment.

“I think the Democrats and Republicans are both spending a disproportionate amount of their budgets on broadcast TV at this point,” said Danielle Butterfield, a Democratic strategist and the executive director of Priorities USA. “Because you can see so clearly what’s happening on the other side, there’s this muscle memory needing to chase and match.”

Political consultants and television executives argue that while broadcast TV may not be what it once was, those ads can reach a larger swath of the population more quickly than through other media. And that audience watching their nightly news programs, not to mention their favorite sitcoms, dramas and football games, is a devoted one.

“Local anchors and reporters are trusted, familiar voices,” said Gregg Siegel, senior vice president of national sales at Sinclair Broadcast Group, one of the country’s largest owners of local TV stations. “They don’t just cover the communities they serve. They live there, raise their families there and are part of the fabric of those communities. That connection creates a level of credibility that is difficult to replicate on other platforms.”

The amount of money being spent on political advertising this election cycle is staggering, helping to boost the bottom lines of the biggest local broadcasting companies like Sinclair, Nexstar Media Group, Gray Media, Tegna and the E.W. Scripps Company.

The research firm S&P Global projects broadcast television advertising this year to be 15 percent higher than the last nonpresidential election year in 2022. And political ad revenue alone is expected to account for 16.3 percent of total broadcast revenue for the year, which would be a record for a nonpresidential election year.

During this election cycle, total political advertising is expected to reach $11.6 billion by Election Day, according to AdImpact; $5.6 billion (48 percent) is flowing to broadcast. That dollar figure is even higher than the one during the 2024 presidential race, when $5.3 billion was spent on broadcast advertising, still 48 percent of the total.

That growth is an outlier in the overall advertising market, where TV’s share continues to shrink as do the overall dollars. In 2024, for example, TV made up 15 percent of all ad spending in the United States, according to the research firm eMarketer. This year, projections envision that figure to be 10 percent.

Nowhere is the broadcast TV blitz more evident than in Texas, where more than half a billion dollars will be spent in the Senate runoff, primaries and general election campaigns.

Oscar Rodriguez, the president of the Texas Association of Broadcasters, said stations in all 20 media markets across the state were seeing ad buys, rather than just a few individual markets. “This is an election where clearly every single vote is going to matter,” he said.

In the tight Senate race between Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate, and James Talarico, his Democratic opponent, $220 million had been spent on broadcast ads through Oct. 28, more than half of the total spending, according to AdImpact. The Paxton campaign and its Republican allies account for most of the broadcast TV outlays, and much of that has been supported by Elon Musk, the world’s richest man with deep business ties to Texas.

Nick Maddux, a senior adviser to Mr. Paxton, said that it was most efficient for the campaign to spend money on linear television because of federal rules that ensure candidates (and at least for now, political parties and joint fund-raising committees) get low-cost TV ad rates.

The campaign’s statewide ad onslaught in October resulted in some ad breaks airing three Paxton spots for every one Talarico ad.

“You go big and fast,” Mr. Maddux said.

Luke Warford, a Democratic political consultant in Texas and chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party, said the Talarico campaign had focused more on building Mr. Talarico’s brand on social media. But the campaign and its Democratic allies have still spent heftily on broadcast TV, devoting 45 percent of their budgets to the medium through Oct. 28, according to AdImpact. (Republicans are at 60 percent.)

Advertising on television can be a blunt force approach to reaching prospective voters, particularly in House races where viewers are often bombarded with ads for candidates in districts not their own. Danilo Yanich, a University of Delaware professor who runs the school’s Local Television News Project, said that’s a trade-off campaigns and PACs will take. “They’ll tolerate those inefficiencies because they’re not sure which voters they will not reach if they try to do those directed kinds of advertising campaigns.”

“Local television viewers are very serious voters,” he added.

And the people who watch broadcast television are often those who vote.

“The kinds of people who tend to be very likely to vote in midterm elections tend to lean older,” Joshua Kalla, a professor of political science at Yale, said. “And those people still watch a whole bunch of broadcast TV.”

There’s another incentive driving this advertising strategy: money. Consultants and media buying firms typically take up to a 15 percent commission on their ad buys, which, given some of the multimillion dollar spends, can quickly add up.

Aaron Evans, a Republican campaign consultant, said that while broadcast had historically “been the beast that moves the numbers,” it was getting less effective every election cycle.

“The thing that is making that industry really outlast its effectiveness is the fact it’s been a cash cow for these consulting firms for decades,” he said.

Some political operatives bemoan what they see as an outdated approach to advertising. During this year’s primaries, several candidates who were vastly outspent on TV ads still prevailed, including Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed over his Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, in Michigan.

Ms. Butterfield, the Democratic strategist, pointed to internal research from Priorities USA that found that 83 percent of registered voters reported in using YouTube and 82 percent used streaming services in a single week in September, while just 61 percent said they watched linear TV. She said that ads on digital platforms, which were much cheaper than TV ads, could see a higher reach and have a more targeted impact.

“The biggest difference between a broadcast television strategy and a digital strategy is how much the campaign actually uses the internet to not just broadcast and shout at a voter, but understand where that voter is, what they care about,” she said.

Mr. Warford, the Democratic political consultant, said Tuesday’s vote would help answer a question about the broadcast television-heavy ad strategy in support of Mr. Paxton. “Is there an amount of money that can save an incredibly weak candidate in a tough environment at the end?”

item.title: Binance Reports $3.64 Billion in Outflows as It Resumes Normal Transactions
item.description:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Sunday that it had begun allowing users to withdraw money, three days after it froze assets in the wake of a cyberattack. Withdrawals initially spiked, as the exchange saw an outflow of $3.64 billion, but then stabilized, Binance said.

The movement was relatively small, Binance said, representing just 2.1 percent of the $171 billion in assets that it manages.

The announcement was an effort to reassure Binance’s users after hackers stole $6.3 billion in digital coins on Thursday, in what appears to be the biggest crypto heist to date. In the wake of the hack, Binance halted withdrawals.

“Our team continues testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets,” Binance said in a post on social media. “We know how important safe and reliable access to your funds is and will share details of the next phase as soon as we can. Rest assured that market conditions are stable.”

Binance said that it would cover all losses that occurred during the hack and that it had worked with other cryptocurrency firms to freeze about $3 billion in stolen assets.

Cybersecurity analysts and the Federal Bureau of Investigation have attributed the hack to North Korea, which has targeted cryptocurrency companies for years, taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their infrastructure to steal assets. The hackers may have used artificial intelligence technology to accelerate their attack, according to the crypto analytics firm Chainalysis, which said that the attackers processed “thousands of transactions in a short period.”

After Binance began allowing users to conduct transactions again, users deposited $1.01 billion and withdrew about $4.65 billion in assets, the company said. Most of those transactions occurred in the first few hours after trading was restored.

“Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times,” Changpeng Zhao, a co-founder of Binance, said in a post on X on Sunday. “Thank you for your trust!”

item.title: After Tech Sell-Off, Investors Brace for More Market Volatility
item.description:
Following last week’s steep sell-off of technology stocks, investors are bracing for further market turbulence at the start of this week, as they await several marquee corporate earnings reports and the results of the U.S. midterm elections.

Futures on the S&P 500, which allow investors to bet on the market before the official start of trading, rose slightly on Sunday night. In Asia, Australian stocks and Japan’s benchmark index fell slightly.

The moves follow sharp losses at the end of last week, fueled by a sell-off in some of the well-known technology companies that have helped boost the stock market to a series of record highs in recent months.

Investors remain concerned about the amount of money the technology companies are spending to build the infrastructure to power artificial intelligence. Those concerns have intensified as companies have increasingly turned to debt markets to finance their spending, adding to the pressure on the companies should the immediate demand for A.I. fall short of expectations.

As companies have reported their financial results for the three months through September, investors have been paying particularly close attention to how much more money company executives think they will need to spend, balancing it against whether revenues have grown sufficiently from the money the companies have already spent.

Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and Amazon, which together account for four of the five “hyperscalers” driving the A.I. buildout, have all seen revisions to their lofty valuations in recent weeks, with investors punishing any appearance of profligacy. The average tech company has fallen 3 percent the day after it reported earnings for the three months through September, by far the worst tech performance of any quarter since Jefferies, an investment bank, started tracking the data 12 years ago.

“Said another way, downside moves have been far more exacerbated than upside moves,” said Jeffrey Favuzza, an analyst at Jefferies.

Apple and Palantir both report earnings after the stock market closes on Monday. Advanced Micro Devices, a chip designer similar to the behemoth Nvidia, reports on Tuesday.

Other, smaller semiconductor companies also report earnings this week, which will help give investors a broader sense of the health of the industry. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell over 15 percent in October and is 27 percent below its record high in June, deep into a bear market, defined as a loss of 20 percent or more from a recent high.

Some analysts think the sell-off has now run its course, and that the technology sector is due for a rebound.

“The risk-reward is now in favor of tech again,” analysts at Deutsche Bank wrote in a research report at the end of last week.

Slowing A.I. growth expectations have helped lower longer-dated interest rates, with the 10-year Treasury yield, which underpins borrowing costs across corporate and consumer debt, falling below 5 percent last week, from a peak of 5.3 percent earlier in October.

The Treasury Department will release its latest borrowing projections this week, with many investors expecting the agency to at least discuss the potential for reducing the size of longer-dated bond sales. That would lower the supply of new bonds for investors to buy, which, in theory, should help pull government interest rates — and therefore yields — down further.

But some analysts warn that this could also create volatility in the government bond market if investors are disappointed by what the Treasury proposes.

Then there are Tuesday’s midterms. If the Democrats gain a majority in either the House or the Senate, investors expect them to rein in President Trump and possibly slow economic growth at the same time; a Republican victory would likely mean the administration would enable the administration to continue with its agenda.

But historically, such policy predictions and how they will affect financial markets tend not to matter. Investors mostly like the clarity that the results of political elections bring with them.

According to the Franklin Institute, the S&P 500 has averaged a 14.9 percent gain over the 12 months after a midterm election, based on the 10 midterms under a Republican president since 1954, with similar market moves regardless of whether Republicans or Democrats take control of Congress.

“Investors have a tendency to believe that politics heavily influence equity markets,” said Chris Galipeau, head market strategist at Franklin Institute. “The reality is quite different historically after midterm elections.”

item.title: FIFA Quietly Paid Millions in Taxes for Its President
item.description:
A typically dry meeting of the three-person committee that determines the pay of FIFA’s most senior officials was winding down in Bangkok one day in May 2024 when one member brought up what he considered a pressing matter.

Bruno Chiomento, a Swiss accountant, noted that FIFA’s president, Gianni Infantino, had relocated from Switzerland to Miami — where he would face higher income taxes — ahead of the 2026 World Cup. FIFA should pay to offset that extra tax burden through 2026, Mr. Chiomento argued. The other members quickly agreed without much further discussion, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times. FIFA would ultimately pay 100 percent of Mr. Infantino’s tax bill to the U.S. government.

A decade ago, an international corruption scandal nearly brought the end of soccer’s global governing body and vaulted Mr. Infantino into power. FIFA introduced sweeping transparency reforms in response, including a bylaw requiring that the compensation of top leadership be made public.

But to the consternation of several senior officials, the tax benefit approved in the Bangkok meeting was never disclosed in filings, according to documents reviewed by The Times and two people familiar with the benefit, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to discuss internal matters. By the time Mr. Infantino’s American assignment is over, FIFA will have paid about $4 million of his taxes. Mr. Infantino earns about $6 million per year, according to FIFA’s annual report.

“All FIFA’s internal regulations and processes, and all applicable laws, have been followed,” FIFA said in a statement. “FIFA ensures all reporting and taxation requirements are met.” FIFA declined to provide further detail about its tax arrangement with Mr. Infantino, but it added that any payments to senior management were independently audited.

Mr. Infantino has courted controversy in recent years over how he has run the top institution for the world’s most popular sport, including his courtship of President Trump, his business dealings on behalf of FIFA and efforts to steer the World Cup to Saudi Arabia.

He is now facing his biggest crisis, after news emerged in July that he secretly held talks to sell a share of World Cup rights to a company owned by the brother of Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law. A global outcry followed, with governments and global soccer officials calling into question his suitability to continue running the 122-year-old institution. He is standing for re-election in March.

The U.S. tax arrangement fits a broader pattern of Mr. Infantino’s benefiting personally at FIFA with the help of people who themselves have received perks, including weekslong trips to the recent World Cup, complete with travel, luxury accommodation and access to the most prestigious areas of the stadiums, the documents show.

Mr. Chiomento, the former chairman of Ernst & Young’s Swiss unit who first raised the tax matter, has known Mr. Infantino for years. He received advice from outside experts — including David Zollinger, Mr. Infantino’s personal lawyer, documents show. FIFA’s own administrative staff had concerns about a conflict of interest in hiring Mr. Zollinger, but the organization still called on his services for several issues that could affect his client.

FIFA declined to comment on why figures connected to Mr. Infantino advised on his personal tax affairs. Mr. Chiomento did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Mr. Zollinger, citing attorney-client privilege, also declined to comment.

During the Bangkok meeting, Mr. Chiomento argued that since FIFA, which has its headquarters in Zurich, had agreed to pay any additional taxes for about a dozen staff members who needed to move to the United States to prepare for the 2026 World Cup, it should do the same for Mr. Infantino. Still, some senior FIFA officials have questioned not only the calculation that Mr. Infantino should contribute nothing toward his American tax bill but also the message it sent about the privileges enjoyed by the organization’s most senior figures.

FIFA’s staff members had received tax advice from a separate group of experts that did not include Mr. Zollinger, the FIFA president’s lawyer, according to the documents.

As FIFA’s chief of governance, compliance and audit, Mr. Chiomento holds outsize influence over Mr. Infantino’s tenure as president — a position amplified by his concurrent role as chairman of the compensation committee. He has also been called upon to weigh in on other sensitive matters involving the president.

One arose this year before the World Cup. Mr. Infantino unilaterally chose to replace FIFA-assigned drivers with GRIZ Global Solutions, a security firm run by an American Special Forces veteran that bills itself as providing “tier one” service to the world’s most important people. He then requested that the same level of service be provided for his wife throughout June and July, covering the period of the tournament, the documents show. When asked to approve that additional agreement, Mr. Chiomento agreed within hours.

FIFA would spend hundreds of thousands of dollars with GRIZ. Internally, at least one official questioned the necessity of providing Mr. Infantino’s wife such services, the documents show. The daily rate was $1,300 per Griz agent, not including the cost of cars, drivers and other expenses.

At the World Cup, Mr. Chiomento, an avid soccer fan, was everywhere. He ensured as much by receiving the equivalent of a V.I.P. pass — a privilege not afforded to any of the dozens of members of committees like his, according to two people with direct knowledge of the arrangement. Dressed in an official FIFA suit reserved for its most senior officials, featuring the organization’s insignia embossed in gold on the breast pocket, he attended any match of his choosing. Mr. Chiomento also traveled on special FIFA charter flights between games, as did Mr. Zollinger and members of Mr. Infantino’s family.

“The governance framework and internal processes put in place by FIFA are robustly applied to the hiring, remuneration and involvement of external service providers, as well as to its guest management operations,” FIFA said in its statement.

The gold-lettered suit is not the only distinction FIFA has bestowed on Mr. Chiomento.

His role had a salary of $250,000. FIFA then changed it to 250,000 Swiss francs, boosting his income by about $50,000 because of currency exchange rates. Salaries for all the other committee heads remain in dollars.

FIFA has turned to other acquaintances of Mr. Infantino for other sensitive assignments, too. In 2024, when the organization redrafted its governing statutes, it called upon Mr. Zollinger and Gianni Rizzello, a lawyer not on FIFA’s staff who studied law at the University of Fribourg at the same time as Mr. Infantino, to help draft them. Those revisions formally increased Mr. Infantino’s presidential powers, which had been curtailed under the reforms he had once championed.

FIFA subsequently tapped Mr. Rizzello to help draft the compensation and benefits policy for FIFA’s most senior executives. He sought Mr. Infantino’s direct input on the revisions even though the policy directly affected the president personally, the documents show.

The policy, approved just before the World Cup, eased restrictions on giving and receiving gifts; loosened rules on V.I.P. invitations; and granted greater discretion over the use of private jets, a mode of transport Mr. Infantino uses frequently as FIFA has an agreement with Qatar’s national carrier. It also arranged, for the first time ever, for FIFA to pay thousands of dollars in fixed compensation to the leaders of a number of advisory committees introduced under Mr. Infantino. The timing alarmed some members of FIFA’s administrative staff, said two people with direct knowledge of the discussions, who worried that the payments could give the impression of currying favor with officials who would vote in the coming election.

The new policy also expanded housing benefits for Mr. Infantino. Under it, the president could request FIFA-funded accommodation in any location where the organization maintains an office — a footprint that has swelled under Mr. Infantino to include offices in Panama, Barbados, Indonesia and Morocco.

FIFA was already paying roughly $600,000 a year to rent a house for him in Miami in addition to an apartment in Switzerland, having also rented one for him in Paris. After moving to Miami in 2023, Mr. Infantino lived for more than two years in a $27 million waterfront mansion owned by the former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt. Matthew Hiltzik, a spokesman for Mr. Schmidt, confirmed that Mr. Infantino had resided there for about three years and paid market rates. Since then, the FIFA president has lived in an apartment that a Delaware company bought from the singer Marc Anthony for $8.6 million last fall. It’s unclear who owns the company.

Mr. Rizzello declined to comment, citing client confidentiality. He also enjoyed V.I.P. access to the World Cup courtesy of FIFA. And he attended a private celebration at a restaurant in Zurich in March marking 10 years of Mr. Infantino’s presidency alongside the president’s inner circle, including Mr. Zollinger, his wife and their blue-eyed Border collie.
